061ad740-a084-11f1-8a09-0bcd9cc59371.one_liner: A macro strategist argues September Fed-hike odds are underpriced and unpacks the term-premium/yield-curve mechanics of a hike, but most of the episode is equity/AI sector rotation with limited direct relevance to financing books.
061ad740-a084-11f1-8a09-0bcd9cc59371.recap: Warren Pies of 314 Research explains why he cut a long-standing bullish equity and commodity overweight to neutral, citing a deteriorating market structure (single-stock volatility collapsing from 50-80% pre-earnings to roughly 35%, correlations still historically low) heading into an August 15-October 15 window loaded with macro risk: a live FOMC meeting, Jackson Hole, potential AI-lab IPOs, and midterm elections. His central rates argument is that the market has swung September hike odds from 75% in July down to 30% and back to roughly 40%, and that his CPI/PPI-driven core PCE nowcast (0.28% m/m) suggests the disinflation narrative is weaker than priced, with political pressure on the Fed (citing Hammack and Waller commentary) potentially tipping the committee toward a hike despite a soft-looking jobs report. He rejects the popular view that a hike would push the 10-year down by restoring credibility, pointing to the ACM term premium (~80bp) and a 2s10s curve near 45-50bp as showing no credibility risk priced in, and cites a historical rule from seven prior hike cycles: every 25bp hike has produced roughly a 20bp rise in the 2-year and 12bp in the 10-year (a bear flattener), with SOFR futures tracking the 10-year in lockstep for two years. He also dismisses Bessent's claim that AI-linked corporate issuance is crowding out Treasuries, arguing issuance relative to GDP and market cap remains low historically. The remainder covers equity sector rotation — semis vs. software, AI capex ROI, GPU rental-rate data, energy as a portfolio hedge — which is largely equity-strategy color.
terms: ACM term premium -- the Adrian-Crump-Moench model's estimate of the extra yield investors demand for holding longer-dated Treasuries beyond expected future short rates
PCE -- Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge
SOFR -- Secured Overnight Financing Rate, the primary US repo-based reference rate

783efb90-5c50-4890-8acc-bf92b8206122.one_liner: A consumer-confidence and retail-discounting deep dive arguing the labor market is quietly deteriorating and disinflation (not inflation) is the real risk -- useful macro background for a rates view but has no direct repo/funding/credit content.
783efb90-5c50-4890-8acc-bf92b8206122.recap: The host argues that a coordinated wave of retail discounting -- Walmart cutting prices on 11,000+ items, Kroger cutting prices on thousands of products, grocery promotions up 10% year-on-year, Amazon pushing into cheap groceries, Aldi/Lidl expanding, and Dick's Sporting Goods stock falling 27% on guidance tied to a 'promotional' sneaker market -- reflects weakening consumer purchasing power rather than resilient demand. The evidence cited: the Conference Board's preliminary August consumer confidence index fell to 89.4, but its forward-looking expectations sub-index dropped to 68.2, deep below the historical 80-level recession threshold. He links this to labor-market data: July payrolls fell 23,000, prior months revised down a combined 103,000, the household survey showed larger declines, participation fell to 61.4%, and an alternative calculation adding an estimated 3.8 million labor-force dropouts implies an 'effective' unemployment rate near 6.2% versus the official 4.1%. He argues this constitutes a slow 'no-hire, some-fire' contraction distinct from NBER-style recessions, which is why confidence indicators have been dismissed. On prices, he notes core CPI's two- and three-month annualized rates hit fresh cycle lows even after a modest July rebound, arguing this shows tariff/energy cost pressures are not generating a broad inflationary second-round effect, but instead demand destruction and margin compression -- consistent with what he says the yield curve is already pricing, contrary to mainstream inflation and 'resilient labor market' narratives.
terms: CPI -- Consumer Price Index, a measure of the average change in prices paid by consumers
NBER -- National Bureau of Economic Research, the body that officially dates U.S. recessions
